Why is the copper oxidized and the silver reduced and not the other way around? As we have seen, substances differ in how readily they gain or lose electrons. The most electronegative element, fluorine, strongly attracts electrons and is very easily reduced. Lithium, on the other hand, has a very low electronegativity, does not attract electrons, and is very easily oxidized. We can order substances in terms of their relative ability (or

) to gain—or to lose—electrons. Our convention is to order substances by their standard reduction potentials: how readily they gain electrons relative to other substances. When we do this, we find that silver gains electrons much more easily than copper. Silver therefore has a higher reduction potential than copper, and when silver and copper couples are connected in an electrochemical cell, silver will be reduced and copper will be oxidized.
